references.text: Joseph turns away from his brothers and weeps, the first time he hides his feelings – a direct parallel to 43:30 where he again withdraws to weep.
Joseph can no longer hold back his emotions and weeps aloud so that the whole house hears it. This is the climax of the emotional development that begins in 42:24 and 43:30.
Joseph falls on Benjamin's neck and weeps, and kisses all his brothers. The love he concealed in 43:30 is now expressed openly.
The mother's inner being was 'moved' (נִכְמְרוּ רַחֲמֶיהָ) over her child – the same rare Hebrew expression used for Joseph's feelings toward Benjamin.
God says, 'My heart turns within me; all my compassion is aroused' (נִכְמְרוּ נִחוּמָי). The same Hebrew root כמר is used for God's deep compassion for His people.
Both verses illustrate Joseph's enduring compassion and weeping in the face of his brothers' fear of revenge.
Both verses show Joseph's deep emotional outburst when he can finally be honest with those closest to him.
This verse is the direct continuation of the weeping mentioned in 43:30, where Joseph finally opens up to his brothers.
This is a specific elaboration of Joseph's compassion from 43:30, directed especially toward Benjamin.
This verse describes the emotional breaking point that led to the weeping in 43:30.
A clear theological parallel: Joseph's compassion for his brothers mirrors the Father's compassion in the parable of the prodigal son.
The brothers' admission of guilt (42:21) creates the context for Joseph's deep compassion in 43:30.
